families.topic: provider preparedness and response at each Heat-Health Alert level
families.page_title: Heat-Health Alert action card for health and social care providers
evidence_points: The action card is intended primarily for managers in hospitals, residential social care, fixed-site primary or community care and home-care services.
It includes actions for year-round preparation, pre-summer readiness and yellow, amber and red Heat-Health Alert levels.
NHS organisations, local authorities, Local Health Resilience Partnerships and Local Resilience Forums are expected to use the actions when developing local plans.
Staff should use professional judgement and act immediately when a patient or client is at risk of overheating.
The card identifies older people, young children, pregnant people and people with several underlying conditions among higher-risk groups.
The alert system uses impact and likelihood to assign yellow, amber or red levels.
The core Heat-Health Alert season runs from 1 June to 30 September, with extraordinary alerts possible outside that period.
The card links year-round planning, preparation before summer, prevention, specific hot-weather response, monitoring and evaluation.

evidence_points: The guidance is primarily intended for managers in hospitals, care homes, community health sites and services delivering care in people’s homes.
It separates actions by setting where not every recommendation applies to every provider.
It covers year-round summer preparedness, pre-summer readiness and yellow, amber and red alert actions.
It links summary action cards for home-care services, hospitals and community healthcare, and residential adult social care.
Local organisations are expected to develop plans before summer as part of wider extreme-heat preparedness.
Staff should know the immediate actions required when a patient or client is at risk from an excessively hot home or room.
Professional judgement and the needs of the individual patient or client remain central to implementation.
The guidance applies to England and is designed to complement wider local arrangements.

Surveillance and monitoring systems are recommended to evaluate local hot-weather interventions.
Commissioning processes should explicitly consider preparedness for hot weather.
Licensing authorities should ensure organisers of large summer events assess and mitigate heat risks.
At red alert, local emergency plans and multi-agency coordination should be activated.

families.topic: impact-based heat-health alerting, seasons, planners and alert levels
evidence_points: The Heat-Health Alerting system is part of the Weather-Health Alerting system operated by UKHSA with the Met Office.
It is intended for health and social care professionals, hot-weather responders and the public.
The core alerting season runs from 1 June to 30 September.
An extraordinary alert may be issued if significant heat occurs outside the core season.
Heat-health planners are issued on Mondays and Fridays for short-, medium- and longer-range horizon scanning.
UKHSA and the Met Office carry out a joint dynamic risk assessment when hot weather is identified.
The system has used impact-based alerting since 2023.
Yellow, amber and red alerts combine expected health impact with the likelihood of those impacts.
A forecast, alert, symptom, exposure report, incident notification or checklist alone does not establish that every recommendation on Heat-Health Alerting system applies.
